results.title: Efficient Annotator Reliability Assessment with EffiARA - arXiv.org
results.content: Published Time: Wed, 04 Jun 2025 01:08:54 GMT > arXiv:2504.00589v3 [cs.CL] 3 Jun 2025 # Efficient Annotator Reliability Assessment with EffiARA ## Owen Cook, Jake Vasilakes, Ian Roberts and Xingyi Song ## School of Computer Science, University of Sheffield ## Abstract Data annotation is an essential component of the machine learning pipeline; it is also a costly and time-consuming process. The framework’s effi-cacy is supported by two previous studies: one improving classification performance through annotator-reliability-based soft-label aggrega-tion and sample weighting, and the other in-creasing the overall agreement among annota-tors through removing identifying and replac-ing an unreliable annotator. We introduce the EffiARA (Efficient Annota-tor Reliability Assessment) framework, which sup-ports annotation quality assessment and manage-ment throughout the annotation process, allowing users to: • Distribute data points to annotators; • Generate labels from the annotations of each annotator; • Assess agreement among annotators; • Assess annotator reliability ;• Redistribute data points to obtain the desired level of agreement; • Generate aggregated labels at the data point level, taking either a soft- or hard-label ap-proach. Assessing annotator reliability can be used to as-sess the quality of individual annotators and may be used to understand the quality of data avail-able, remove low-reliability annotators (Cook et al., 2025), inform the training of machine learning models through aggregating soft labels with relia-bility (Dawid and Skene, 1979; Wu et al., 2023), or affect the loss function during training (Cao et al., 2023; Cook et al., 2024). The source code is available at 2Figure 1: An overview of the EffiARA annotation pipeline, covering sample distribution, annotation, label generation, agreement calculation, reliability estimation, and dataset compilation. Once resources have been finalised, data points can be distributed among annotators with the EffiARA distribution algorithm, which ensures annotator agreement can be effectively assessed (Cook et al., 2024). In the work introducing the Effi-ARA annotation framework (Cook et al., 2024), utilising reliability scores in the label generation and model training stages was shown to improve classification performance. This work utilises the EffiARA reliability scores to identify unreliable annotators during the annotation process, lead-ing to an increased overall level of agreement among annotators, which is highly indicative of data quality (Krippendorff, 2018).

results.title: Efficient Annotator Reliability Assessment with EffiARA
results.content: The framework’s efficacy is supported by two previous studies: one improving classification performance through annotator-reliability-based soft-label aggregation and sample weighting, and the other increasing the overall agreement among annotators through removing identifying and replacing an unreliable annotator. Annotator reliability can also be used to dynamically weight individual data points during model training to ensure that the model prioritises reliable annotations (Cook et al., 2024). Assessing annotator reliability can be used to assess the quality of individual annotators and may be used to understand the quality of data available, remove low-reliability annotators (Cook et al., 2025), inform the training of machine learning models through aggregating soft labels with reliability (Dawid and Skene, 1979; Wu et al., 2023), or affect the loss function during training (Cao et al., 2023; Cook et al., 2024). There are different approaches to assessing annotator reliability, such as learning through Expectation Maximisation (Cao et al., 2023) or directly inferring the reliability of an annotator from their agreement with others (Inel et al., 2014; Dumitrache et al., 2018; Cook et al., 2024, 2025). It distributes samples to annotators, generates and aggregates labels, computes inter- and intra-annotator agreement, and assesses annotator reliability. Once resources have been finalised, data points can be distributed among annotators with the EffiARA distribution algorithm, which ensures annotator agreement can be effectively assessed (Cook et al., 2024). Once labels for each annotation have been generated, inter- and intra-annotator agreement are calculated using equations introduced in Cook et al. Once the desired level of agreement has been reached, potentially with the aim of generating gold-standard labels in classification tasks, the final dataset is ready, with annotations tied to annotator identities, allowing for training strategies that utilise the expertise and reliability of individual annotators. Two previous works involving dataset creation have annotated data following the EffiARA methodology, creating RUC-MCD (Cook et al., 2024) and the Chinese News Framing dataset (Cook et al., 2025). In the work introducing the EffiARA annotation framework (Cook et al., 2024), utilising reliability scores in the label generation and model training stages was shown to improve classification performance. This work utilises the EffiARA reliability scores to identify unreliable annotators during the annotation process, leading to an increased overall level of agreement among annotators, which is highly indicative of data quality (Krippendorff, 2018).

I want to calculate kappa score for a multi label image classification problem. import sklearn sklearn.metrics.cohen_kappa_score(y_test, predictions). ## 2 Answers 2. Krippendorff’s alpha (also called Krippendorff’s Coefficient) is an alternative to Cohen’s Kappa for determining inter-rater reliability. Although Krippendorff's Alpha isn't available in sklearn library you can use it using this package krippendorff. import krippendorff reliability_data = [[prediction matrix],[ground truth]] print(krippendorff.alpha(reliability_data=reliability_data)). answered Aug 31, 2019 at 17:31. Can you describe that in your answer please? the `krippendorff.alpha(reliability_data)` takes in a single matrix , but i have two matrices, predictions and true labels. here reliability\_data = [[prediction matrix],[ground truth matrix]]. import krippendorff reliability_data = [[predictions], [y_test]] print(krippendorff.alpha(reliability_data=reliability_data, level_of_measurement='nominal')). results.title: Inter-annotator reliability (Cohen's kappa) - ELAN - The Language Archive Forums
results.content: I have two questions regarding the calculation of the inter-annotator reliability using Cohen’s kappa. 1. Is it possible to calculate inter-annotator reliability only with reference two one single value of the controlled vocabulary? Since one tier has 100% “x” and the other 82%, I would expect a strong inter-annotator reliability result, even in the case segmentation differs between the two tiers. The outcome could be quite similar to what you got so far (except maybe for those annotation values that occur only a few times compared to most other values, see e.g. the Limitations section of the kappa Wikipedia page). Anyway, if you want to try that, you could maybe use e.g. the `Tier->Copy Annotations from Tier to Tier` to create 2 new tiers both containing only the value you are interested in (that function has such an option).
